[2026-15665: lines 1935-2334 of 6220, FR page 49193]
  1935      Commenter 0115 expressed concern that excluding probationary and 
  1936  temporary employees from RIF procedures might hurt efforts to recruit 
  1937  early-career talent. However, probationary, trial period, and temporary 
  1938  employees are the most likely to be separated under the current RIF 
  1939  rules, which require agencies to place these employees at the bottom of 
  1940  the retention register due to their lack of tenure and seniority. The 
  1941  changes in this rulemaking make it much more likely that an agency will 
  1942  be able to retain these employees post-restructuring, as the decision 
  1943  to retain or separate these employees would no longer depend on their 
  1944  retention standing.
  1945      Commenter 0683 urged OPM to consider the impact of the exclusion of 
  1946  probationary employees from RIF procedures on leadership pipeline 
  1947  investments, and to recommend that agencies account for leadership 
  1948  development considerations in their workforce planning. OPM agrees that 
  1949  agencies should closely consider the impact on leadership pipelines in 
  1950  determining whether agencies should release probationary employees in a 
  1951  reduction in force. Indeed, OPM notes that the regulatory flexibility 
  1952  to exclude probationary employees from RIF procedures is essential to 
  1953  protecting investments that agencies have made in recruiting 
  1954  outstanding early career employees.
  1955      Commenters 0037 and 0678 argued that the changes remove procedural 
  1956  protections from these employees, while Commenters 0680 and 0672 
  1957  referenced past instances where probationary employees were allegedly 
  1958  subject to termination without regard to their
  1959  
  1960  [[Page 49194]]
  1961  
  1962  performance. However, probationary, trial period and temporary 
  1963  employees will continue to be protected by the Merit System Principles 
  1964  codified in 5 U.S.C. 2301, which require that Federal employees receive 
  1965  fair and equitable treatment in personnel management without regard to 
  1966  political affiliation, and that they receive protection against 
  1967  arbitrary action or coercion for partisan political purposes. In 
  1968  addition, probationary and trial period employees will also continue to 
  1969  be subject to applicable procedures under Civil Service Rule 11, while 
  1970  probationary employees would be able to appeal their terminations to 
  1971  OPM under the proposed rule ``Streamlining Probationary and Trial 
  1972  Period Appeals'' (90 FR 61070). In addition, in the final rule, OPM is 
  1973  revising Sec.  351.202(d) to note specifically that actions to retain, 
  1974  furlough, separate, demote or reassign employees excluded from RIF 
  1975  competition must be consistent with the terms of the employee's 
  1976  appointment and applicable law, and that such employees must be 
  1977  provided a modified RIF notice.
  1978      Thus, these changes will not subject probationary and trial period 
  1979  employees to arbitrary action, retaliation, or pretextual decision-
  1980  making without redress. Instead, the changes make it more likely that 
  1981  these employees could be retained post-restructuring and recognize 
  1982  relevant differences between these categories of employees and others 
  1983  (namely, their limited performance history) while maintaining the 
  1984  procedural rights appropriate to their employment.
  1985      Commenter 0685 urged that OPM adopt a presumption of retention for 
  1986  probationary employees. OPM does not adopt this suggestion, as the 
  1987  subject of probationary employment is covered comprehensively in E.O. 
  1988  14284 and Civil Service Rule 11 (5 CFR part 11), which provide clear 
  1989  processes for evaluating probationary employees. In addition, OPM notes 
  1990  that the Merit System Principles codified in 5 U.S.C. 2301 and OPM's 
  1991  parallel rulemaking regarding appeals for probationary employees 
  1992  provide further protections for this group of employees.
  1993  3. Emergency Shutdown Furloughs
  1994      OPM is modifying the definition of the term furlough in Sec.  
  1995  351.203 to exclude an emergency shutdown furlough caused by a lapse in 
  1996  congressional appropriations where the ultimate duration of the 
  1997  furlough is not known by the agency at the outset of the furlough. 
  1998  Commenters generally supported this change. Commenter 0687 noted that 
  1999  because ``Congress has subsequently guaranteed backpay to federal 
  2000  employees in a law signed by President Trump in 2019'' and thus ``all 
  2001  employees are eventually compensated by law for time they would 
  2002  otherwise be at work'' (unlike in the case of an unpaid RIF furlough), 
  2003  a RIF furlough notice should not be required in emergency shutdown 
  2004  furloughs. Commenter 0686, a Federal agency, commented that ``[t]his 
  2005  change improves efficiency and ensures employees are not subject to 
  2006  repeated, unnecessary notices when a furlough is based on a lack of 
  2007  appropriations.'' In the final rule, OPM is making a minor, non-
  2008  substantive change to remove the limitation that the length of the 
  2009  furlough must be ``dependent entirely on congressional action, rather 
  2010  than agency action'' to avoid confusion (as agencies often call 
  2011  employees back to work during government shutdowns of unknown length 
  2012  that are caused by lapses in appropriations).
  2013  4. Transfers of Function
  2014      OPM is revising Sec.  351.203 to modify the definition of transfer 
  2015  of function to adhere to the text of the applicable statute enacted by 
  2016  Congress to govern transfers of function, 5 U.S.C. 3503. That statute 
  2017  only applies to a situation ``[w]hen a function is transferred from one 
  2018  agency to another . . . .'' (emphasis added).
  2019      Commenters 0672 and 0674 argued that narrowing transfer-of-function 
  2020  procedures would weaken employee protections and allow agencies to 
  2021  evade RIF rules through internal reorganizations. OPM disagrees. This 
  2022  rule does not allow agencies to evade RIF requirements when an internal 
  2023  reorganization results in release from a competitive level for RIF 
  2024  reasons. Rather, it distinguishes between interagency transfers of 
  2025  function, where governmentwide transfer-of-function protections are 
  2026  statutorily required, and internal management realignments, where 
  2027  ordinary reassignment principles can address any resulting personnel 
  2028  actions and offer adequate protections for employees. Specifically, 
  2029  transfers and reassignments of employees in the competitive service 
  2030  within agencies will continue to be governed by 5 CFR part 335. 
  2031  Transfers and reassignments of employees within agencies in the 
  2032  excepted service will continue to be governed by 5 CFR parts 213 and 
  2033  302. Further, 5 U.S.C. 2301 requires agencies to adhere to Merit System 
  2034  Principles in personnel management, including transfers and 
  2035  reassignments of employees, and in the final rule OPM is amending Sec.  
  2036  351.204 to provide specifically that its 5 CFR part 351 regulations 
  2037  must be administered and applied consistent with all applicable laws, 
  2038  including the Merit System Principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b).
  2039      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, stated that ``[t]he updated 
  2040  definition for transfer of function will remove constraints that 
  2041  currently impede timely organizational adjustments,'' noting that 
  2042  existing rules result in ``administrative obstacles that slow [its] 
  2043  ability to adapt quickly to emerging needs.'' Commenter 0719 noted 
  2044  that, ``[u]nder existing regulations, even straightforward internal 
  2045  realignments can require extensive procedures, discouraging agencies 
  2046  from implementing changes that could reduce duplication, improve 
  2047  efficiency, or better align staff with mission priorities.'' OPM 
  2048  agrees.
  2049  5. Other Definitions
  2050      In this rule, OPM is providing a formal definition of ``reduction 
  2051  in force'': the release of a competing employee from his or her 
  2052  competitive level by furlough for more than 30 days, separation, or 
  2053  demotion, or reassignment requiring displacement, when the release is 
  2054  required because of lack of work; shortage of funds; insufficient 
  2055  personnel ceiling; reorganization; or the exercise of reemployment 
  2056  rights or restoration rights. OPM did not receive significant comments 
  2057  regarding its definition of ``reduction in force,'' as this definition 
  2058  closely tracks the longstanding coverage of OPM's RIF regulations, as 
  2059  reflected in 5 CFR 351.201(a)(2).
  2060      This rule modifies the current definitions in Sec.  351.203 for 
  2061  current rating of record and rating of record. The revision to current 
  2062  rating of record updates the cross reference within part 351. The 
  2063  revision to rating of record clarifies that only the annual performance 
  2064  evaluation--and not a mid-year within-grade evaluation--can be used 
  2065  when computing the performance credit, which is used for determining 
  2066  standing on the retention register. OPM did not receive significant 
  2067  adverse comment regarding these changes.
  2068      OPM is also adding meanings for agency, Government obligation and 
  2069  military spouse, and to correct a typo in Sec.  351.204 to change 
  2070  ``reduction force'' to ``reduction in force.'' OPM did not receive 
  2071  significant adverse comment regarding these proposed changes. As 
  2072  discussed further below, OPM is also adding a definition for 
  2073  restoration protected employee.
  2074      Commenter 0687 suggested that OPM add an anti-manipulation 
  2075  provision to state clearly that agencies may not manipulate competitive 
  2076  areas to purposefully target employees in ways
  2077  
  2078  [[Page 49195]]
  2079  
  2080  that are inconsistent with Merit System Principles. OPM agrees, in 
  2081  part, and is adding a provision to Sec.  351.204, setting forth the 
  2082  responsibilities of agencies, to clarify that agencies are not only 
  2083  responsible for following and applying the RIF regulations, but for 
  2084  ensuring that such regulations are administered and applied consistent 
  2085  with the Merit System Principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b). OPM 
  2086  agrees with Commenter 0687 that ``[t]his issue is the crux of what OPM 
  2087  has historically attempted to do with its regulations.''
  2088  
  2089  B. Part 351, Subpart C: Changes in Transfer of Function Procedures
  2090  
  2091      OPM is substituting the word ``agency'' for ``competitive area'' 
  2092  throughout subpart C and making other conforming changes, so as to 
  2093  align with the text of the statute Congress enacted governing transfers 
  2094  of functions (5 U.S.C. 3503), which applies to transfers of functions 
  2095  between agencies, not within agencies. Notably, the regulations 
  2096  governing transfers of function applicable to the SES apply only to 
  2097  ``the transfer of the performance of a continuing function from one 
  2098  agency to one or more other agencies.'' 5 CFR 359.608 (emphasis added); 
  2099  see also 5 U.S.C. 3595 (providing to the SES rights comparable to those 
  2100  provided by 5 U.S.C. 3503). Similarly, OPM's regulations in Sec.  
  2101  353.109 regarding restoration to duty from uniformed service or 
  2102  compensable injury only speak of transfers between agencies.
  2103      Commenter 0687 suggested that ``OPM should require agencies to 
  2104  provide advance notice and the opportunity to follow one's function 
  2105  when functions are transferred between competitive areas within a 
  2106  single agency, even if the full transfer-of-function procedures of 
  2107  Subpart C are not required.'' OPM disagrees. It believes that agencies 
  2108  will appropriately seek to retain talented and knowledgeable employees 
  2109  during intra-agency transfers of function even without a regulatory 
  2110  requirement to provide advance notice and the opportunity to transfer 
  2111  when a function is transferred within a single agency. OPM believes 
  2112  that this current regulatory requirement unduly inhibits agencies from 
  2113  carrying out internal restructurings and generates litigation without a 
  2114  corresponding benefit to the government.
  2115      OPM is revising Sec.  351.302(b) to remove the unclear term 
  2116  ``liquidation'' and make the meaning of this section more plain by 
  2117  adapting language from OPM's Workforce Reshaping Handbook explaining 
  2118  its practical operation. OPM did not receive significant adverse 
  2119  comment regarding this provision and is therefore finalizing it. In 
  2120  addition, in this rule, OPM is revising Sec.  351.302(b) to state that, 
  2121  except as permitted in paragraph (e) of this section, the losing agency 
  2122  must use the adverse action procedures found in 5 CFR part 752, if 
  2123  applicable, or other procedures required by law, regulation, or the 
  2124  terms of the employee's appointment, if it chooses to separate a 
  2125  competing employee who declines to transfer with his or her function. 
  2126  That is because some employees affected by transfer-of-function 
  2127  procedures may not be covered by part 752, and some separations may be 
  2128  governed by other procedures.
  2129      OPM is revising Sec.  351.302(g) to clarify the procedures that 
  2130  agencies must follow in asking employees whether they wish to transfer 
  2131  with the function, when functions are transferred between agencies. OPM 
  2132  is also revising Sec.  351.303 to simplify the process for identifying 
  2133  which employees are identified with the transferring function. OPM did 
  2134  not receive significant adverse comment regarding these provisions and 
  2135  is finalizing them.
  2136  
  2137  C. Part 351, Subpart D: Changes in How Competitive Areas Are Defined 
  2138  and Approved
  2139  
  2140      This rule revises Sec.  351.402(b) to allow agencies to designate a 
  2141  competitive area as being any organizational unit, or combination of 
  2142  organizational units, on an agency's official organizational chart. 
  2143  Organizational charts must be available on the agency's public facing 
  2144  web page or otherwise appropriately documented by the agency. An 
  2145  organizational unit for these purposes must be designated/approved by 
  2146  the head of the agency, or designee, and the designation or approval 
  2147  cannot be redelegated to an official below the agency's headquarters 
  2148  level.
  2149      In addition, OPM is revising Sec.  351.402(b) to require that an 
  2150  organizational unit for purposes of a RIF must be clearly distinguished 
  2151  from other organizational units with regard to its operation, work 
  2152  function, staff, and supervisory oversight. In addition, OPM is 
  2153  clarifying that field or regional offices officially established by the 
  2154  agency as discrete organizational units and shown on the agency's 
  2155  official organizational chart may be their own competitive area(s).
  2156      Commenter 0684 contended that the previous regulatory phrase 
  2157  ``under separate administration'' was not vague but had an accepted 
  2158  meaning as encompassing ``the authority to take or direct personnel 
  2159  actions.'' Commenter 0684 argued that the requirement in this rule that 
  2160  an organizational unit be differentiated from other organizational 
  2161  units with regard to its operation, work function, staff, and 
  2162  supervisory oversight is not equivalent to the previous phrase.
  2163      However, the previous OPM rulemaking and Federal Circuit case cited 
  2164  by Commenter 0684 state that ``under separate administration'' may be 
  2165  satisfied by as little as the authority to ``assign duties,'' a power 
  2166  that any front-line supervisor would possess. Further, OPM's current 
  2167  Workforce Reshaping Operations Handbook rejects Commenter 0684's 
  2168  definition of ``under separate administration,'' as OPM states that the 
  2169  definition ``[r]ecognizes that individual organizational components may 
  2170  be under separate administration even though many agencies reserve 
  2171  final approval of certain personnel actions to a higher level in the 
  2172  agency.'' \15\ Ultimately, Commenter 0684 only underscores that the 
  2173  phrase ``under separate administration'' is confusing, and that OPM was 
  2174  correct in the proposed rule in stating that ``the current terminology

  2262      As noted above, under this rule (and particularly Sec.  351.501

  2264  placed on a RIF retention register, agencies will now do so based on

  2271  the longer service will be ranked ahead.

  2273  groups for both the competitive and excepted services. The competitive 
  2274  service tenure group will consist of all competitive service employees

  2280  213.101) who are not serving a trial period and are not serving in a 
  2281  temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.

  2283  each career employee in the competitive service who, as of the date the 
  2284  employee receives a specific reduction in force notice, is not serving 
  2285  an initial probationary period. This definition is substantially the 
  2286  same as the current competitive service tenure group I.
  2287      Competitive service tenure subgroup II will consist of every other 
  2288  competitive service employee who, as of the date of the RIF notice, is 
  2289  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary or term 
  2290  appointment of 1 year or less. For example, an employee serving under a 
  2291  career-conditional competitive service appointment who has completed a 
  2292  probationary period but not yet completed the service requirements for 
  2293  career tenure (under 5 CFR 315.201) would be included in subgroup II.

  2297  specific reduction in force notice, are not serving a trial period and 
  2298  whose appointment carries no restriction or condition such as 
  2299  conditional, indefinite, or specific time limit. This definition is 
  2300  substantially the same as current excepted service tenure group I.

  2438      New paragraph Sec.  351.503(e) Multiple rating patterns addresses 
  2439  situations in which an agency has employees in a competitive area who

  2444  transmuting or assigning an employee a higher summary level rating than 
  2445  what he or she received under a previous rating system when there is 
  2446  documented evidence of exceptional or higher-level performance 
  2447  consistent with the criteria in revised Sec.  351.503(d).
  2448      In addition, for an employee who goes from an appraisal system 
  2449  which uses a higher pattern of summary levels to a lower one (e.g., an

  2454  the retention register who does not have documented evidence of 
  2455  exceptional performance as described above. This method allows agencies 
  2456  to adopt policies that would prevent exceptional performers from being 
  2457  disadvantaged because they may be covered under two or more patterns of 
  2458  summary rating levels which may not make meaningful distinctions for 
  2459  performance among employees. Further, Sec.  351.503 will require RIF 
  2460  performance ratings and assigned summary levels, including adjustments, 
  2461  to be uniformly and consistently applied within the competitive area 
  2462  and consistent with the agency's implementing issuances. Where an 
  2463  agency elects to assign additional performance credit, the agency must

  2467  factor performance ratings into the RIF process when an employee does 
  2468  not have three actual ratings of record during the 4-year period prior

  2475      Section 351.504 Veterans' preference defines how veterans' 
  2476  preference will be applied in a RIF in both the competitive and 
  2477  excepted services. Each preference eligible employee with a compensable 
  2478  service-connected disability of 30 percent or more will receive an 
  2479  additional 5 points added to their performance credit, while every 
  2480  other preference eligible employee will receive an additional 3 points 
  2481  added to their performance credit. ``Preference eligibles'' is defined 
  2482  in 5 U.S.C. 2108(3) to include not only veterans, but also certain

  2486      Commenter 0660 asserted, without any additional information, that 
  2487  ``the proposed rules are vague and unclear as to exactly how 
  2488  performance and veterans' issues are to be determined,'' but does not 
  2489  indicate in what manner the proposed rule is vague or unclear, 
  2490  providing no supporting information whatsoever. Commenter 0660 
  2491  contended that ``[t]he proposed regulation will make it likely that the

  2496      OPM disagrees with Commenter 0660's assertions. The current rules 
  2497  require agencies to categorize employees based on tenure group and 
  2498  veterans' preference subgroup. Employees are ranked first by tenure 
  2499  group I, II, III; then within each tenure group by veterans' preference 
  2500  subgroup AD, A, B; and only then by years of service as augmented by 
  2501  performance credit, starting with the earliest service date. Agencies 
  2502  then prepare an ``adjusted SCD'' calculation where extra years of 
  2503  service are added to an employee's actual service computation date. 
  2504  That means current RIF ordering is not a simple comparison of Employee 
  2505  A's performance against Employee B's performance. Agencies must first 
  2506  place employees into tenure groups, then veterans' preference 
  2507  subgroups, then calculate adjusted service dates. Performance affects 
  2508  ranking only inside the employee's already-determined tenure/veterans' 
  2509  preference category.
  2510      Agencies then must undergo multiple rounds of complicated bumping 
  2511  and retreating before arriving at a final retention register. Notably, 
  2512  ``bump and retreat'' can create a chain. If Employee A bumps Employee 
  2513  B, then Employee B is released from that competitive level, and the 
  2514  agency must determine whether Employee B has his or her own bump or 
  2515  retreat right. This process is highly burdensome and prone to errors.
  2516      This rule replaces the current rules with a streamlined system that 
  2517  eliminates the need for multiple, complicated rounds of bump and 
  2518  retreat, replacing it with a straightforward comparison of employee 
  2519  performance as augmented by veterans' preference, with ties broken by 
  2520  tenure and length of service. Further, OPM's new rules are simpler 
  2521  because they eliminate the most confusing features of the current 
  2522  rules: using performance to manufacture an adjusted service computation 
  2523  date and complicated bump-and-retreat procedures.
  2524      This rule addresses that problem by making performance credit more 
  2525  transparent and direct: Level 5 ratings receive 7 points, Level 4 
  2526  ratings receive 5 points, Level 3 ratings receive 3 points, and Level 1 
  2527  or 2 ratings receive no points. Veterans' preference is then added to 
  2528  that performance credit.
  2529      This rule's use of defined point values--Level 5 = 7 points, Level 
  2530  4 = 5 points, Level 3 = 3 points, and Level 1 or 2 = 0 points--also 
  2531  makes the RIF calculation easier to understand and audit than an 
  2532  artificial performance-adjusted SCD. As Commenter 0687 noted, this 
  2533  reform simplifies the composition of retention registers.
  2534      In addition, this rule does not change the basic record-keeping 
  2535  requirements in current Sec.  351.505 (renumbered to Sec.  351.506) or 
  2536  the notice requirements in Sec.  351.802, except to conform their 
  2537  provisions to other changes made in this rulemaking. Thus, OPM does not 
  2538  agree with Commenter 0678's assertion that the rule ``reduces notice 
  2539  and transparency'' regarding RIFs. Instead, OPM agrees with Commenter 
  2540  0687, who noted that the revisions ``simplify[ ] the composition of 
  2541  retention registers . . . such that retention standing is faster to 
  2542  compute, more transparent, and more equitably applied.''

  2546      In the proposed rule, OPM provided order of retention examples. 
  2547  Commenter 0680 points out correctly that some of the tables 
  2548  illustrating the operation of the proposed rule contained errors, as 
  2549  they incorrectly ranked employees in a higher tenure subgroup ahead of 
  2550  employees with a greater performance credit. OPM is therefore 
  2551  correcting these examples below. OPM is also publishing further 
  2552  examples of how retention standing will work under the new regulations 
  2553  to aid with administration of the new rules.
  2554      OPM disagrees with Commenter 0680 that these inadvertent errors 
  2555  show a lack of reasoned decision-making, that the new rules increase 
  2556  the risk of mistakes, or that OPM or agencies are unprepared to 
  2557  administer the new rules. Such a correction is consistent with ordinary 
  2558  rulemaking practice: agencies often revise, add, delete, or correct 
  2559  examples to conform them to the operative regulatory standard or to 
  2560  respond to comments.\16\ The binding rule is the regulatory text, which 
  2561  provides that employees are ranked by performance credit as augmented 
  2562  by veterans' preference, with tenure subgroup and service computation 
  2563  date used as tie-breakers. The proposed rule text clearly stated that, 
  2564  within each tenure group, employees are ranked by performance credit as 
  2565  augmented by veterans' preference, and only when employees have the 
  2566  same augmented performance credit are they further ranked by tenure 
  2567  subgroup and then by length of service.
  2568      Indeed, OPM believes the new RIF formula is much simpler to 
  2569  understand and apply than the current formula, as it involves a simple 
  2570  calculation of performance credits adjusted for veterans' status, with 
  2571  tenure subgroup and length of service serving as tiebreakers. The 
  2572  current system, by contrast, involves a multi-layered system where 
  2573  employees were sorted into three tenure groups, with veterans' status 
  2574  subgroups within each tenure group, with employees then further sorted 
  2575  by service computation date that is adjusted based on performance. That 
  2576  process required agencies to translate performance into years, average 
  2577  the credited years, round where necessary, and then move the employee's 
  2578  service date backward to create an ``adjusted SCD.'' That made the 
  2579  register harder to understand because the service computation date was 
  2580  not the employee's actual service date, but an artificial service date 
  2581  reflecting both service and performance. Further, agencies were then 
  2582  required to engage in complicated ``bump and retreat'' exercises 
  2583  between employees in different tenure groups, often encompassing 
  2584  multiple rounds of RIF competition governed by detailed rules that were 
  2585  understood by very few beyond a very small group of Federal HR 
  2586  specialists and consultants.
  2587      Under this rule, by contrast, performance remains a score that 
  2588  corresponds to direct numerical values, augmented by consistent 
  2589  numerical values for veterans' preference. Thus, the new rules will 
  2590  likely result in far fewer errors than the old rules. They are also 
  2591  easier and more streamlined, making them easier to apply and understand 
  2592  by both HR offices and Federal employees. Employees who inspect the 
  2593  register will be much more likely to understand how their retention 
  2594  standing was calculated and be able to spot errors.
  2595      Several commenters agree that the new regulations are simpler than 
  2596  the current ones. Commenter 0687 noted that the new rule simplifies the 
  2597  composition of retention registers and the application of assignment 
  2598  rights, versus the current complicated ``bump and retreat'' process. 
  2599  Commenter 0685 noted that the benefits of OPM's simplification of RIF 
  2600  rules are ``substantial and should not be understated,'' and that ``the 
  2601  proposal's effort to simplify the RIF framework represents a meaningful 
  2602  and constructive reform.''

  2828  and does not require the agency to redetermine or recalculate retention 
  2829  standing under subpart E. This amendment affirms the necessary 
  2830  consequence of the changes to Sec.  351.507: once retention standing is

  2835  E. Part 351, Subpart F: Furloughs, Abolishment of Competitive Area, 
  2836  USERRA Rights, and Exceptions
  2837  
  2838      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.601 for consistency with how retention 
  2839  standing is to be calculated under Subpart E of part 351. OPM is also 
  2840  modifying Sec.  351.602 to remove the prohibition on retaining an 
  2841  employee serving a specifically limited temporary appointment in a 
  2842  competitive level while releasing a competing employee from that level. 
  2843  OPM did not receive significant adverse comments on these provisions 
  2844  and is finalizing them.
  2845  1. RIF Furloughs
  2846      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to modify its regulations in 
  2847  Sec.  351.604 regarding furloughs of more than 30 consecutive calendar 
  2848  days (or more than 22 workdays if done on a discontinuous basis over a 
  2849  period not exceeding 1 year) to remove the requirement that agencies 
  2850  furlough employees based on retention standing and recall employees to 
  2851  duty from furlough based on retention standing.
  2852      Commenter 0687 opposed these changes, contending that they had ``no 
  2853  obvious use case and could create mechanisms for abuse.'' Commenter 
  2854  0687 noted that agencies typically do not engage in unpaid furloughs of 
  2855  any length, whether greater or less than 30 days, and that OPM's 
  2856  proposed revision would create risks that agencies could use long 
  2857  furloughs to circumvent normal RIF procedures. Commenter 0687 therefore 
  2858  contended that the risks of this new provision outweigh the benefits. 
  2859  Commenter 0117 similarly expressed concern that agencies could use 
  2860  long-term unpaid furloughs to avoid following retention order 
  2861  requirements. OPM agrees that its proposed changes to Sec.  351.604 
  2862  warrant further consideration and has chosen not to finalize them.
  2863  2. Abolishment of a Competitive Area
  2864      In this rule, OPM is renaming Sec.  351.605 as Abolishment of a 
  2865  competitive area to more accurately describe its purpose. The revised 
  2866  section explains that the appropriate use of this provision is when an 
  2867  agency is abolishing all positions (including the positions of 
  2868  employees otherwise excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  
  2869  351.202(d)) in a competitive area within 180 days. It further explains 
  2870  that, because all positions in the competitive area will be eliminated, 
  2871  an agency is not required to release competing employees in order of 
  2872  retention standing.
  2873      As the D.C. Circuit explained in upholding an earlier version of 
  2874  this provision, when all employees in a competitive area will be 
  2875  released within a relatively short time, ``it is certainly reasonable 
  2876  to conclude that it would be a waste of resources for an agency to be 
  2877  forced to perform detailed seniority and performance calculations 
  2878  solely to construct a rank ordering of employees' retention rights when 
  2879  those rights are of such little value.'' AFGE v. OPM, 821 F.2d at 766 
  2880  n. 4. Thus, OPM was ``within its authority to conclude that under those 
  2881  limited circumstances, no effect is `due.' '' Id. With performance now 
  2882  the main consideration governing RIF retention, the same considerations 
  2883  apply: it does not make sense to require agencies to perform detailed 
  2884  seniority and performance calculations to construct a rank ordering of 
  2885  employees that will have no substantive effect on their retention 
  2886  rights.
  2887      In this final rule, OPM is making minor wording and ordering 
  2888  changes to this provision. Section 351.605(c) provides that any 
  2889  competing employee released under this provision must be provided a 
  2890  specific written notice in accordance with Sec.  351.801, Notice 
  2891  period. The notice must include the following: the action being taken 
  2892  and its effective date; the competitive area being abolished; a link to 
  2893  5 CFR part 351 and access to the agency's records pertinent to the RIF 
  2894  being run to abolish the competitive area; information on reemployment 
  2895  rights; the employee's appeal rights; and a statement that, because all 
  2896  positions in the competitive area are being abolished pursuant to 5 CFR 
  2897  351.605, the employee was not ranked relative to other competing 
  2898  employees in the reduction in force. The notice is not required to 
  2899  include the information described in Sec.  351.802(a)(2) or (a)(4).
  2900      Section 351.605(d), Retention register not required, explains that 
  2901  an agency is not required to rank competing employees in the abolished 
  2902  competitive area, and must not apply the assignment right provisions in 
  2903  subpart G, because
  2904  
  2905  [[Page 49203]]
  2906  
  2907  no positions in the competitive area will remain.
  2908      Commenter 0683 suggested that OPM review and approve any 
  2909  competitive area abolishment due to the potential that agencies could 
  2910  use this provision alongside the new competitive area definition to 
  2911  evade the need to build a retention register and provide assignment 
  2912  rights. OPM believes that these concerns are adequately addressed by 
  2913  the requirement in Sec.  351.402(c) that OPM approve new or 
  2914  substantially modified competitive areas that have been in effect less 
  2915  than 90 days prior to the issuance of RIF notices; the requirement in 
  2916  Sec.  351.204 that agencies must administer and apply the regulations 
  2917  consistent with all applicable laws, including the Merit System 
  2918  Principles in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b); the requirement that the competitive 
  2919  area be disclosed to the employee in the RIF notice; and the 
  2920  availability of RIF appeal rights in Subpart I of 5 CFR part 351.
  2921      Commenter 0683 also asked that OPM clarify that the abolishment of 
  2922  a competitive area under Section 351.605 does not diminish or supersede 
  2923  the statutory placement rights of career SES members under 5 U.S.C. 
  2924  3594-3595. OPM confirms that these revisions are not intended to 
  2925  diminish or supersede career SES placement rights in a RIF. However, 
  2926  OPM believes that 5 CFR 359.602(b) is clear enough on this point that 
  2927  no change to the regulatory text in 5 CFR part 351 is required.
  2928  3. USERRA Rights
  2929      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to modify Sec.  351.606(a), 
  2930  which addresses mandatory RIF exceptions for employees who have been 
  2931  restored or reemployed following uniformed service and who remain 
  2932  entitled to post-reemployment retention protection under Sec.  
  2933  353.209(b) for either 6 months or 1 year. These retention rights are 
  2934  provided under USERRA.
  2935      Commenter 0686, a Federal agency, requested that OPM clarify the 
  2936  proposed modifications to Sec.  351.606, and particularly its 
  2937  interaction with Sec.  351.605, which revises the procedures to be 
  2938  followed when a competitive area is abolished. Several other commenters 
  2939  (0076, 0121, 0455, 0550, 0597) argued that the proposed rule could be 
  2940  read as undermining USERRA rights, including where an employee 
  2941  performing uniformed service or recently reemployed after uniformed 
  2942  service lacks recent civilian performance ratings.
  2943      OPM agrees that clarification is appropriate. Accordingly, OPM in 
  2944  this final rule is making explicit how USERRA restoration and retention 
  2945  protections operate when an employee is affected by a RIF.
  2946      First, OPM is adding a definition of ``Restoration protected 
  2947  employee'' in Sec.  351.203. For purposes of part 351, a restoration 
  2948  protected employee is a competing employee who has been restored or 
  2949  reemployed following uniformed service and who, as of the date the 
  2950  employee receives a specific reduction in force notice, remains within 
  2951  the 6-month or 1-year post-reemployment protection period described in 
  2952  Sec.  353.209(b). Those protection periods implement 38 U.S.C. 4316(c), 
  2953  which provides that a person reemployed under USERRA may not be 
  2954  discharged from employment, except for cause, for 1 year after 
  2955  reemployment if the period of uniformed service was more than 180 days, 
  2956  or for 180 days after reemployment if the period of service was more 
  2957  than 30 days but less than 181 days.
  2958      Second, OPM is revising Sec.  351.606 to clarify that agencies must 
  2959  apply USERRA retention protections and restoration rights as a 
  2960  mandatory exception to the ordinary RIF order of release. The agency 
  2961  must first determine the employee's ordinary retention standing under 
  2962  subpart E. The agency must then apply the mandatory exception in Sec.  
  2963  351.606(a). During the applicable 6-month or 1-year protection period, 
  2964  the agency may not release a restoration protected employee from the 
  2965  competitive level if another competing employee may be released 
  2966  instead.
  2967      Third, OPM is clarifying how the mandatory exception applies when 
  2968  an agency abolishes all positions in a competitive area under Sec.  
  2969  351.605. When an entire competitive area is abolished pursuant to Sec.  
  2970  351.605, the agency may not separate the restoration protected employee 
  2971  by RIF during the applicable 6-month or 1-year protection period. 
  2972  Instead, the employee must be assigned by the agency to a different 
  2973  position of like seniority, status, and pay for which the employee is 
  2974  qualified, consistent with 5 CFR part 353.
  2975      Fourth, OPM is revising Sec.  353.209(a) to conform part 353 to 
  2976  these part 351 clarifications. Section 353.209(a) already provides that 
  2977  an employee performing duty with the uniformed services may not be 
  2978  demoted or separated, other than military separation, except for cause; 
  2979  that RIF is not ``for cause'' under that subpart; that the employee is 
  2980  not a competing employee under part 351; and that, if the employee's 
  2981  position is abolished during the absence, the agency must reassign the 
  2982  employee to another position of like status and pay. OPM is clarifying 
  2983  that this reassignment obligation applies when the employee's position 
  2984  is abolished in a RIF, including when all positions in the employee's 
  2985  competitive area are abolished under Sec.  351.605.
  2986      Fifth, OPM is clarifying the relationship between part 351, part 
  2987  353, and 38 U.S.C. 4314 when the employing agency can no longer place 
  2988  the employee. If the employee's function has been transferred to 
  2989  another agency, the employee's rights are governed by the transfer and 
  2990  restoration provisions in 5 CFR part 353. If the employing agency no 
  2991  longer exists and its functions have not been transferred, or if it is 
  2992  impossible or unreasonable for the agency to reassign the restoration 
  2993  protected employee, OPM will offer placement assistance elsewhere in 
  2994  the executive branch to the employee pursuant to 5 CFR 353.110.
  2995      These revisions also address concerns that employees performing 
  2996  uniformed service, or recently returned from uniformed service, may 
  2997  lack recent civilian ratings of record. This rule's missing-rating 
  2998  provisions continue to address how ordinary performance credit is 
  2999  calculated for competing employees who do not have three ratings of 
  3000  record, including use of the modal rating for employees with no ratings 
  3001  during the relevant four-year period and proxy rules for employees with 
  3002  one or two ratings. But for a restoration-protected employee within the 
  3003  6-month or 1-year post-reemployment protection period, the mandatory 
  3004  exception in Sec.  351.606(a) operates independently of the employee's 
  3005  ordinary retention standing. Thus, the employee is not penalized for 
  3006  lacking recent civilian ratings during the protected period; the agency 
  3007  must honor the USERRA retention protection before releasing the 
  3008  employee by RIF.
  3009      In addition, this rule preserves credit for uniformed service in 
  3010  calculating length of service for RIF purposes. Section 351.505(b)(1) 
  3011  provides that all active duty in a uniformed service, as defined in 5 
  3012  U.S.C. 2101(3), is creditable for purposes of part 351, except as 
  3013  otherwise provided in that section. The service computation date 
  3014  includes all actual creditable service under Sec.  351.505(a) and (b).
  3015  4. Exceptions

    91  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
    92  
    93  I. Executive Summary
    94  
    95      OPM is revising its regulations governing RIFs and making related 
    96  changes to its regulations under statutory authority found at 5 U.S.C. 
    97  1103, 1104, 1302, 3304, 3320, 3330, 3502, 3503, 3596, 4305, and 4315, 
    98  and 38 U.S.C. 4331. The rule makes the following changes:
    99      1. Replaces the current tenure-group framework with a simplified 
   100  competitive service and excepted service structure. The rule 
   101  consolidates current tenure groups I, II, and III into a ``competitive 
   102  service tenure group'' and an ``excepted service tenure group,'' with 
   103  two subgroups in each.
   104      2. Excludes certain employees from RIF competition. Employees 
   105  serving initial probationary periods, trial periods, temporary or time-
   106  limited appointments of one year or less, and Schedule C and Schedule G 
   107  employees are not ``competing employees'' for RIF purposes and can be 
   108  retained, furloughed, separated, demoted, or reassigned without using 
   109  RIF procedures.
   110      3. Reorders retention standing to place performance first. Agencies 
   111  will maintain separate retention registers for competitive service and 
   112  excepted service employees; within each group, employees will be ranked 
   113  by performance credit, augmented by veterans' preference, with tenure 
   114  subgroup and length of service used as tie-breakers.
   115      4. Creates a new numerical performance credit methodology. Agencies 
   116  will calculate performance credit using the three most recent ratings 
   117  of record from the relevant four-year period, assigning 7 points for 
   118  Level 5, 5 points for Level 4, 3 points for Level 3, and 0 points for 
   119  Level 1 or Level 2 ratings, with special rules for missing ratings and 
   120  differing appraisal patterns.
   121      5. Applies veterans' preference by adding points to performance 
   122  credit. Preference eligibles with a compensable service-connected 
   123  disability of 30 percent or more receive 5 additional points; other 
   124  preference eligibles receive 3 additional points; non-preference 
   125  eligibles receive no additional points.
   126      6. Adds definitions of key terms. The rule defines ``competing 
   127  employee,'' ``competitive service tenure group,'' ``excepted service 
   128  tenure group,'' ``reduction in force,'' ``initial probationary 
   129  period,'' ``trial period,'' ``government obligation,'' and ``military 
   130  spouse.''
   131      7. Excludes emergency shutdown furloughs from the RIF furlough 
   132  definition. The rule excludes emergency shutdown furloughs caused by 
   133  lapses in appropriations from the RIF furlough definition.
   134      8. Removes erosion of duties reclassifications from actions 
   135  requiring RIF procedures, while adding an anti-manipulation safeguard. 
   136  Agencies will no longer need to use RIF procedures for such 
   137  reclassifications but could not undertake an erosion of duties 
   138  reclassification after announcing a RIF if it would adversely affect an 
   139  employee's retention standing.
   140      9. Narrows and simplifies transfer-of-function requirements. The 
   141  rule narrows transfer-of-function requirements to transfers between 
   142  agencies, rather than transfers within a single agency, and simplifies 
   143  identification of employees tied to a transferring function by focusing 
   144  on whether the employee performs the function at least half of the 
   145  time.
   146      10. Clarifies how agencies define competitive areas. Under this 
   147  rule, competitive areas may be based on official organizational units 
   148  or combinations of units. Agencies may define certain geographic 
   149  locations as separate competitive areas, while employees working at 
   150  approved alternate locations remain assigned to their official 
   151  organizational unit for competitive area purposes. In addition, an 
   152  organizational unit for RIF purposes must be clearly distinguished from 
   153  other organizational units with regard to its operation, work function, 
   154  staff, and supervisory oversight.
   155      11. Clarifies and simplifies procedures when an entire competitive 
   156  area is being abolished. When abolishing all positions in a competitive 
   157  area within 180 days, agencies may release employees without ranking 
   158  them on a retention register or applying assignment rights, and with a 
   159  simplified notice.
   160      12. Revises and simplifies assignment rights by replacing ``bump 
   161  and retreat'' concepts with assignment rights to a position held by an 
   162  employee with a lower-retention-standing. A released employee in the 
   163  competitive service will receive assignment rights to a qualifying 
   164  position held by another employee with lower retention standing in the 
   165  same tenure group, generally within three grades below the released 
   166  employee's position, or five grades for certain 30-percent-or-more 
   167  disabled veterans.
   168      13. Requires skills-based assessments for RIF assignment 
   169  qualifications and RPL selection. Agencies must assess whether 
   170  employees or RPL candidates have the capacity, adaptability, and skills 
   171  needed for the position through job-related assessments based on job 
   172  analysis (unless the employee held the same or substantially similar 
   173  position within five years of the RIF and achieved a rating of Level 3 
   174  (Fully Successful), or higher, or equivalent, for performing the duties 
   175  of the position). This change requires agencies to use more rigorous 
   176  assessments in accordance with the Chance to Compete Act of 2024 (Pub. 
   177  L. 118-188) to determine whether the individual is qualified.
   178      14. Updates RPL, CTAP and ICTAP rules to conform to the new RIF 
   179  framework. The rule replaces references to prior tenure groups with the 
   180  new competitive service tenure group, preserves preexisting eligibility 
   181  through OPM-recognized qualifying appointments, updates selection 
   182  methods to emphasize skills-based assessments, and adds exceptions 
   183  allowing agencies to retain or finalize appointments of probationary 
   184  employees.
   185  
   186  [[Page 49179]]
   187  
   188      15. Updates Pathways and post-secondary student regulations to 
   189  conform to the new RIF framework. The rule modifies regulations in 5 
   190  CFR parts 316 and 362, pertaining to post-secondary students and 
   191  Pathways Programs, to clarify how such appointments are treated for RIF 
   192  purposes in conformance with the changes made by this rule.
   193      16. Revises RIF exceptions, notices, and records, and makes various 
   194  conforming changes in other regulatory sections. The rule clarifies 
   195  continuing and temporary exceptions allowing agencies to retain 
   196  employees who would otherwise be separated via a RIF, including for 
   197  government obligations, parental leave, sick-leave-related 
   198  circumstances, annual leave, and military spouses; fixes retention 
   199  standing as of the date the employee receives a specific RIF notice 
   200  (rather than the date the RIF is executed); updates required notice 
   201  content; and makes conforming changes for post-secondary students, 
   202  Pathways interns, compensable-injury restoration rights, Senior 
   203  Executive Service (SES) furloughs, and performance management cross-
   204  references.
   205      In addition, in this rule, OPM is modifying the proposed rule in 
   206  the following ways:
   207      1. Clarifying how retention and restoration rights under the 
   208  Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 
   209  (USERRA) apply in a RIF. In response to public comments, this rule 
   210  provides additional clarity regarding how USERRA applies to RIFs. It 
   211  requires that agencies apply USERRA retention protections and 
   212  restoration rights as a mandatory exception to the order of release 
   213  under a RIF. When an entire competitive area is abolished pursuant to 
   214  Sec.  351.605, an employee entitled to USERRA retention protections or 
   215  restoration rights must be assigned to a different position at the 
   216  agency. If an entire agency is abolished, OPM will provide placement 
   217  assistance elsewhere in the Executive Branch.
   218      2. Reinforcing Merit System Principles. OPM is revising Sec.  
   219  351.204 to clarify that agencies have a responsibility not only to 
   220  follow and apply the regulations in Part 351 when conducting a RIF, but 
   221  to ensure that the RIF regulations are administered and applied 
   222  consistent with all applicable laws, including the merit system 
   223  principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b).
   224      3. Providing additional competitive area safeguards. OPM is 
   225  requiring that, when a competitive area will be in effect less than 90 
   226  days prior to a specific RIF notice, or has been materially modified, 
   227  an agency must submit a description of the competitive area and 
   228  provide, for OPM review, a written explanation of the bona fide 
   229  organizational basis for the competitive area.
   230      4. Clarifying exclusions of employees from RIF competition in Sec.  
   231  351.202(d). The final rule clarifies that if the individuals among the 
   232  categories of employees specified in Sec.  351.202(d) as excluded from 
   233  RIF competition are released for the reasons described in Sec.  
   234  351.201(a)(2) (i.e., lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
   235  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment 
   236  rights or restoration rights), they must receive a modified RIF notice, 
   237  unless the release is the natural expiration of the temporary or time-
   238  limited appointment.
   239      5. Making various clarifying and conforming changes and updating an 
   240  outdated reference. The final rule makes changes to the wording of 
   241  Sec.  351.605, dealing with abolishment of a competitive area, to 
   242  further clarify the meaning of this provision; makes minor changes to 
   243  the definition of ``emergency shutdown furlough'' in Sec.  351.203 and 
   244  Sec.  359.802 to remove potentially confusing language; updates Sec.  
   245  353.110 to replace outdated OPM contact information for placement 
   246  assistance; adds an introductory phrase to Sec.  351.802(a); and makes 
   247  conforming changes to Sec.  351.805, dealing with successive RIF 
   248  notices, and Sec.  362.306, dealing with Pathways recent graduates, to 
   249  ensure consistency with other changes made in this rulemaking.
   250      6. Not finalizing changes to RIF furlough procedures. In response 
   251  to input from public comments, OPM has elected not to finalize a 
   252  further change to provide greater flexibility for agencies to conduct 
   253  unpaid furloughs of more than 30 days.

    90  
    91  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: OPM is issuing this final rule to modernize 
    92  the administrative process for appeals by employees who are furloughed 
    93  for more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force 
    94  action under 5 CFR part 351. Congress charged OPM with prescribing 
    95  regulations governing the release of competing employees in a RIF, and 
    96  OPM has historically implemented RIF appeal procedures through 
    97  regulation. This final rule revises that regulatory framework by 
    98  replacing the prior MSPB forum for future non-SES RIF appeals with a 
    99  uniform OPM-administered process. The rule does not alter agencies' 
   100  responsibility to determine their workforce needs or whether a RIF is 
   101  necessary. By requiring a complete RIF-specific agency record, 
   102  permitting an appellant reply, authorizing additional information, 
   103  audits, investigations, and hearings when necessary and efficient, and 
   104  preserving collateral statutory remedies, the final rule provides 
   105  meaningful administrative review while reducing delay, fragmentation, 
   106  and unnecessary litigation burden.
   107  
   108  I. Digest of Public Comments and Summary of Changes From the Proposed 
   109  Rule
   110  
   111      In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 1,252 comments 
   112  during the 30-day public comment period from a variety of individuals, 
   113  including current and former civil servants, members of Congress, as 
   114  well as organizations, including local and national unions and Federal 
   115  agencies. Of the 1,252 comments, 1,251 were posted on 
   116  www.regulations.gov, and one was not posted because it contained vulgar 
   117  language unrelated to the rulemaking in question. At the conclusion of 
   118  the public comment period, OPM reviewed and analyzed the comments. In 
   119  general, the comments ranged from ardent support of the proposed 
   120  regulation to categorical rejection of it. Less than 1 percent of the 
   121  overall comments were supportive, neutral, or mixed, and 99 percent 
   122  opposed the proposed regulation.
   123      OPM found many of the comments helpful. OPM has revised the final 
   124  rule to clarify, narrow, or supplement the proposed RIF appeal 
   125  procedures in response to comments, including comments concerning 
   126  burden of proof, access to the agency record, information asymmetry, 
   127  due process, neutrality, hearings, protective orders, collective 
   128  bargaining, and public disclosure. In response to those comments, the 
   129  final rule adds more precise appeal standards, a detailed RIF-specific 
   130  agency-record requirement, disclosure and privilege protections, 
   131  stronger adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards, narrower e-
   132  filing sanctions, more flexible reply rules, and more carefully 
   133  tailored protective order and public posting provisions. The revisions 
   134  are summarized below.
   135      Clarifying appealable actions. The final text clarifies the 
   136  appealable actions set forth in Sec.  351.901(a). The proposal allowed 
   137  an employee ``who has been the subject of a reduction-in-force action'' 
   138  to appeal an action taken under part 351. The final text specifies that 
   139  only an employee furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or 
   140  demoted by a RIF action taken under part 351 may appeal that action to 
   141  OPM.
   142      Revising the merits standard. The final text replaces the proposed 
   143  ``would not have suffered the same or another RIF action'' standard in 
   144  Sec.  351.901(b) with a more precise two-part merits showing: the 
   145  appellant must prove that the agency failed to comply with an 
   146  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 
   147  351, and the failure prejudiced the appellant by causing the appealed 
   148  action or the loss of a materially more favorable outcome. This is 
   149  clearer and better focused on prejudicial RIF-compliance error.
   150      Revising exclusivity language. The final text continues to provide 
   151  that part 351 procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing 
   152  a RIF action, and adds that RIFs and matters related to the appeals of 
   153  RIFs cannot be raised in grievance procedures or challenged through 
   154  grievance arbitration, while expressly preserving collateral matters 
   155  within the independent jurisdiction of Equal Employment Opportunity 
   156  Commission (EEOC), Inspectors General, MSPB, Department of Labor 
   157  Veterans' Employment and Training Service (DOL VETS), and the Office of 
   158  Special Counsel (OSC). The final text also retains the no-judicial-
   159  review provision.
   160      Updating filing-system language. The final text replaces the 
   161  proposed placeholder for the electronic filing system with a reference 
   162  to the system identified on OPM's website. It also replaces 
   163  ``statements, evidence, or documents'' with ``pleadings, evidence, or 
   164  documents,'' better aligning the filing provision with adjudicatory 
   165  terminology.
   166      Clarifying filing deadlines. The final text changes the filing 
   167  deadline from 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time to 11:59 p.m. Eastern 
   168  Time, avoiding confusion during daylight saving time. It also 
   169  consolidates the untimely-filing rule in Sec.  351.902(b)(2) and 
   170  provides that good-cause determinations are within OPM's sole and 
   171  exclusive discretion.
   172      Adding a limited tolling rule for collateral matters. The final 
   173  text adds Sec.  351.902(b)(3), which permits an employee who timely 
   174  filed a collateral matter within the independent jurisdiction of an 
   175  entity identified in Sec.  351.901(c) to file a RIF appeal within 30 
   176  calendar days after the final decision on that matter, where that 
   177  decision materially affects the employee's retention standing, order of 
   178  release, assignment rights, or other rights under part 351. The final 
   179  text provides that a decision is final for this purpose when it is no 
   180  longer subject to further administrative review and that OPM 
   181  determines, in its sole and exclusive discretion, whether the decision 
   182  materially affects the employee's rights.
   183      Requiring filing-information detail in the RIF notice. The final 
   184  text amends Sec.  351.802(a)(6) to require the specific RIF notice to 
   185  state, in addition to the employee's right to appeal to OPM, the
   186  
   187  [[Page 49231]]
   188  
   189  time limit for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and the 
   190  electronic filing system through which an appeal must be filed.
   191      Narrowing e-filing enforcement. The final text narrows the proposed 
   192  e-filing enforcement provisions. Rather than authorizing broader orders 
   193  regulating filing methods, sanctions, misuse, or termination of e-filer 
   194  participation, the final text provides that OPM may strike a document 
   195  when an e-filer repeatedly fails to follow filing instructions after a 
   196  show-cause order. The final text also removes the proposed statement 
   197  that withdrawal from e-filing may preclude future re-registration and 
   198  clarifies that withdrawal of e-filing registration is not good cause 
   199  for staying a case.
   200      Simplifying initial-appeal information. The final text simplifies 
   201  the contact-information requirements in Sec.  351.903(a) by replacing 
   202  ``legal name, best address'' with ``name, address.'' The core 
   203  requirement remains unchanged: the appeal must be written, state the 
   204  basis for the appeal, identify the appellant and any representative, 
   205  and include supporting documentation.
   206      Defining the agency record. The final text adds a RIF-specific 
   207  minimum agency-record requirement to Sec.  351.903(b). The proposal 
   208  required the agency response to include the agency record but did not 
   209  define its contents. The final text specifies that the agency record 
   210  includes, at a minimum, the RIF notice and effective-date documents, 
   211  documents supporting the RIF reason, coverage and appointment records, 
   212  competitive-area and competitive-level records, retention-register and 
   213  retention-standing records, order-of-release records, assignment-rights 
   214  records, special RIF-circumstance records, and a certification that the 
   215  complete agency record has been produced.
   216      Distinguishing production to OPM from service on the appellant. The 
   217  final text requires the agency to produce the complete agency record to 
   218  OPM while serving the appellant with the agency record subject to 
   219  legally required limits. The agency may redact or withhold information 
   220  from the appellant's copy only to the extent necessary to comply with 
   221  the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-information or 
   222  national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, or other 
   223  disclosure limits required by law.
   224      Allowing limited new matters in reply. The final text revises Sec.  
   225  351.903(c) to permit an appellant's reply to raise a new allegation of 
   226  error if the basis for that allegation rests on information first 
   227  disclosed in the agency response or if OPM grants leave for good cause.
   228      Adding disclosure limits for inspection and service. The final text 
   229  makes inspection of OPM's appellate record and service of documents 
   230  subject to the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-
   231  information or national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, 
   232  and other applicable disclosure limits required by law. The proposal 
   233  allowed inspection and required service but did not include the same 
   234  express disclosure limitations.
   235      Reorganizing representative provisions. The final text reorganizes 
   236  Sec.  351.904 into separate paragraphs addressing designation of a 
   237  representative, Federal employee representatives and restrictions on 
   238  official time and reimbursement, and disallowance of representatives. 
   239  The final text also narrows the grounds for disallowing a 
   240  representative. Because a Federal employee representative may not 
   241  perform representational functions while in a duty status, the final 
   242  text does not adopt the proposed additional grounds for disallowance 
   243  based on the priority needs of the Government or unreasonable costs to 
   244  the Government; OPM or the responsible agency may disallow an 
   245  employee's choice of representative only where the representative is an 
   246  employee of the responsible agency or OPM and the representative's 
   247  activities would cause a conflict of interest or position. The 
   248  remaining changes are primarily organizational and clarifying.
   249      Adding adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards. The final 
   250  text adds safeguards in Sec.  351.905(a) requiring OPM adjudicators to 
   251  be insulated from officials who participated personally and 
   252  substantially in the challenged action or provided case-specific 
   253  advice. It also prohibits adjudicators from considering material ex 
   254  parte communications on the merits and requires any such communication 
   255  to be summarized in the record with an opportunity for party response, 
   256  unless disclosure is prohibited by law.
   257      Clarifying OPM employee appeals. The final text clarifies that an 
   258  administrative law judge (ALJ) assigned to adjudicate an OPM employee's 
   259  appeal will issue an initial decision. It also adds material factual 
   260  error affecting the outcome as a ground on which OPM may disturb the 
   261  ALJ's decision and clarifies that assigning an ALJ does not make 5 
   262  U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 applicable unless independently required by law 
   263  or expressly incorporated.
   264      Tightening audits and investigations. The final text narrows the 
   265  standard for OPM audits or investigations. The proposal allowed OPM to 
   266  conduct an audit or investigation when the ``interest of justice'' 
   267  would be served. The final text requires OPM to determine that the 
   268  existing record is insufficient to resolve a material issue within 
   269  OPM's jurisdiction and that the audit or investigation is reasonably 
   270  likely to produce material information. The final text also provides 
   271  that representatives may not participate in an audit or investigation 
   272  unless OPM specifically requests it.
   273      Removing a separate ascertainment sanction. The final text removes 
   274  the proposed separate paragraph authorizing sanctions for failure to 
   275  participate in ascertainment of facts and renumbers the initial-
   276  decision and remedies provisions.
   277      Refining protective-order authority. The final text revises Sec.  
   278  351.906(a). The proposal focused on harassing communications and use of 
   279  appeal information for unrelated purposes. The final text authorizes 
   280  protective orders or cease-and-desist directives to protect the 
   281  integrity of the adjudicatory process and to prevent threats, 
   282  intimidation, targeted harassment, improper witness contact, disclosure 
   283  of protected personal information, or misuse of nonpublic information 
   284  obtained through the appeal. It also requires protective orders to be 
   285  no broader than reasonably necessary and not to restrict lawful 
   286  communications protected by law.
   287      Clarifying OPM-initiated reconsideration. The final text clarifies 
   288  in Sec.  351.907(a) that OPM may reopen and reconsider an initial 
   289  decision either upon request of a party or on its own initiative. The 
   290  proposal allowed party-requested reconsideration, while Director sua 
   291  sponte review was addressed separately.
   292      Clarifying Director review. The final text revises Sec.  351.908 to 
   293  preserve the Director's sua sponte authority to reopen and reconsider a 
   294  nonfinal initial decision or reopened and reconsidered decision, while 
   295  identifying nonexclusive considerations that may guide that review. The 
   296  proposal gave the Director broad discretion to reopen and reconsider 
   297  any nonfinal decision. The final text clarifies that the Director may 
   298  consider whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on an 
   299  erroneous material factual finding, involves an issue of exceptional 
   300  importance, affects governmentwide civil service administration, 
   301  conflicts with another OPM decision, or otherwise warrants review. It 
   302  also clarifies that Sec.  351.908 does not create a party right to 
   303  request Director review and that, upon reopening, the Director may take 
   304  any action available under Sec.  351.907(c).
   305  
   306  [[Page 49232]]
   307  
   308      Revising finality of initial decisions. The final text revises 
   309  Sec.  351.909 so that an initial decision becomes final 30 calendar 
   310  days after issuance unless, before that time, a party timely requests 
   311  reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 or the Director 
   312  reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908. A timely request suspends 
   313  finality: if OPM denies or dismisses the request without reopening the 
   314  initial decision, the initial decision becomes final 30 calendar days 
   315  after issuance of the denial or dismissal unless the Director reopens 
   316  it before that time, and if OPM grants the request, the reopened and 
   317  reconsidered decision becomes final 30 calendar days after issuance 
   318  unless the Director reopens that decision before that time. An untimely 
   319  request does not suspend or otherwise affect finality. The final text 
   320  also clarifies that a decision by the Director that disposes of the 
   321  appeal is final and effective upon issuance and that, if the Director 
   322  remands the appeal or directs further proceedings, any resulting 
   323  decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. These changes conform 
   324  finality to the reconsideration and Director-review provisions of the 
   325  final rule.
   326      Adding public-posting disclosure limits. The final text adds 
   327  express legal limits on public posting of final merits decisions, 
   328  including requirements protecting privacy, privileged information, 
   329  protected personnel information, law-enforcement-sensitive information, 
   330  and other information that may not lawfully be disclosed. It also 
   331  clarifies that final merits decisions not publicly posted because of 
   332  such legal limits must be made available upon request to the Federal 
   333  employee or former Federal employee involved in a proceeding under this 
   334  subpart, his or her representative selected pursuant to Sec.  351.904, 
   335  or a representative of the Federal agency or office involved in the 
   336  proceeding who has a need to know.
   337      OPM is finalizing the RIF appeals rule as amended. After 
   338  considering the comments, OPM concludes that the final rule, as 
   339  amended, better balances timely adjudication, governmentwide 
   340  consistency, employee access to meaningful administrative review, and 
   341  agencies' need for finality in workforce restructuring than the current 
   342  MSPB appeal process for non-SES RIFs.
   343  
   344  II. Background

  2159      (a) Upon a request from either party to the dispute, OPM may, in 
  2160  its sole and

  2164  exclusive discretion, reopen and reconsider an initial decision issued

  2214      (c) A decision by the Director pursuant to Sec.  351.908 is the

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

  2279  IV. Section-by-Section Analysis
  2280  
  2281      In this section, OPM discusses the regulatory amendments to 5 CFR 
  2282  chapter I, subchapter B, part 351, subpart I, governing appeals of and 
  2283  corrective action with respect to RIFs.
  2284  
  2285  A. Section 351.802--Content of Notice
  2286  
  2287      OPM is revising Sec.  351.802(a)(6), which governs the information 
  2288  an agency must include in a written notice to an employee affected by a 
  2289  reduction in force. Current Sec.  351.802(a)(6) refers to the 
  2290  employee's right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board. 
  2291  Because this final rule transfers adjudication of covered RIF appeals 
  2292  from MSPB to OPM, revised Sec.  351.802(a)(6) replaces the MSPB 
  2293  reference with a reference to OPM.
  2294      The revised provision requires an agency's RIF notice to inform the 
  2295  employee, as applicable, of the employee's right to appeal to OPM. As 
  2296  revised in this final rule, the notice must also state the time limit 
  2297  for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and identify the electronic 
  2298  filing system, available on OPM's website, through which an appeal must 
  2299  be filed. This requirement preserves the practical filing information 
  2300  previously conveyed through the cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 of 
  2301  this title and forecloses any contention that a RIF notice failed to 
  2302  apprise an employee of how and when to appeal. The provision is 
  2303  conforming in nature and is intended to ensure that employees receive 
  2304  accurate notice of the administrative appeal forum established by 
  2305  revised subpart I. The revision does not eliminate any independently 
  2306  applicable statutory notice requirement or any separately available 
  2307  remedial process administered by another entity.
  2308      The proposed rule retained legacy language in Sec.  351.802(a)(6) 
  2309  requiring agencies to comply with Sec.  1201.21 of this title, as 
  2310  applicable. OPM is removing that cross-reference in the final rule. 
  2311  Section 1201.21 is an MSPB notice provision that applies when an agency 
  2312  issues a decision notice in a matter appealable to the Board. It 
  2313  requires MSPB-specific information, including notice of the time limits 
  2314  for appealing to the Board, the address of the appropriate Board 
  2315  office, access to the Board's regulations, and access to the MSPB 
  2316  appeal form. Because this final rule replaces MSPB with OPM as the 
  2317  adjudicative forum for RIF appeals under part 351, retaining an 
  2318  unqualified cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 in the RIF notice 
  2319  provision could create confusion about where an affected employee must 
  2320  file a RIF appeal.
  2321  
  2322  [[Page 49248]]
  2323  
  2324      This deletion is conforming, clarifying, and nonsubstantive. It 
  2325  does not eliminate any appeal right, shorten any filing period, alter 
  2326  the information an agency must provide about the OPM RIF appeal right, 
  2327  or affect any matter that remains independently appealable to MSPB. 
  2328  Rather, it removes an obsolete MSPB-specific notice cross-reference 
  2329  from a provision that now concerns OPM RIF appeals. To the extent an
